title: Some doubts as aspiring game dev
author: panjezor
selftext:
Hello all!

  
I am a web/app dev with a decade of experience. I've always been interested with how games are built but aside from a few hours with RPG maker 15 years ago, I could only design games on paper or come up with new rules while we were playing tabletops.

I've read plenty of game design resources, watched all of Extra Credits and had my analytical thinking break every game down for past 10 years in hope of understanding what drives each decision. To some it may have been tiring, but I got proper joy from this (ergo games get a bit boring once there is little for me to learn anymore).

I have an idea for an online game, I started a discussion about that game back in 2019 (what game we would all want to play). Over time the idea evolved from a Facebook Messenger chat to a Google Doc document, then to a LaTeX project (65 pages of hand-written content - mostly gameplay features, max 3-4 pages of lore). At some point I managed to put some extra hours into it, migrated LaTeX headers into a private self-hosted mediawiki, total of 602 pages (not dead ones, I average 2.20 edit per page, so its not like i pasted it all and left).

I have the entire game written up, I got all the horizontal/vertical progression figured out, socializing, monetization, gameplay loop - I did have all that 2 years ago.

Once I realized how much content I have, I started working my way through Ulibarri's courses, however after I got midway through the second one, I realized there are UE MCP projects.

Now don't get me wrong, I still do my best to have a proper understanding of the codebase, I did spend my time on a Blender course to figure out how assets are created and optimized.

On the other hand, I have been very passionate about AI since it all started, so as soon as ChatGPT hit v3 I was there trying it out and finding business use and pushing it in the companies I worked at. My previous employer tried to perform some AI revolution too, so our workflow was very experimental just to lead the "race".

Quick jump from then to now - the game is at it's prototype stage, I managed to get the infrastructure, launcher, basic combat, few classes, some monsters, some maps - overall much more than a default indie dev would do 3 years ago. 

But then when I see all the AI hate, I don't see how anything I do with it could succeed? People blame the tool, so any use of it even with good intent does not matter at all, since people get a feel of "this was done with AI" and ultimately get angry at it / the dev.

Is there a way out without sacrificing all the hard work I've put in?

AI is not going away until they jack up the prices for the tokens like 4-5x times and it helped me with so many things already. I'm always planning for long-term and I know some things to make sure it is a well-written application, despite it's just a game. I do plenty of testing, I've automated my CI, I do qualtiy checks on the code that's written, but even then there is still that lingering doubt in my mind saying "people will put an AI label for it and shame it to death, regardless of whether it's a good or a bad game".

I don't need words of support here, I'd rather get some advice from people who have been through that.

comments.author: thecrustycrap
comments.body: Cue 1000th thread about releasing game with ai help and worrying about it, you don’t need advice or support, either you do it with or without ai. Simple

replies.author: panjezor
replies.body:
I mostly saw indie devs developing small games as an alternative to the career.

I treat it as a hobby but at the same time I'm emotionally invested enough to feel less-than-good if it was to flop BECAUSE of the AI label, despite it's quality as a game.

replies.author: VibeForTokens
replies.body:
But do you realistically see yourself completing it without the AI label? As you said above, you are ultimately creating this for yourself. If you enjoy it, then it was a huge success. It's just that simple. 

I'm working on a game that brings back memories of the original of that game type, I'll release it on mobile so I can enjoy it myself. I couldn't care less if anyone buys it. But if people do buy it, that just means the tokens I used to make it were free. Then I work on the next one "I" want to play.

comments.author: Niedzwiedz87
comments.body:
AI is not going anywhere, and soon 99% of games will be developed using AI. There will be no more point in AI hatred; a few people will code without AI for fun, a few people will enjoy their games, but it will be like pottery - a craft, not an industry anymore.

Don't let it discourage you. Developing games is actually going to be an even tougher business, since the entry ticket price has decreased dramatically, and it will be very difficult to make a living out of games. But not because of AI hatred.

Good luck!

replies.author: panjezor
replies.body: I've been saying that once this game launches there will always be at least 1 active player since i am really happy with the gameplay design concepts and worst case scenario I'll rebuild it into a solo-MMO, but I am building this game to play it myself. Absolutely no expectation of being a global success or anything of the sort. Don't need it to be of any decent financial return, to be fair I only thought of monetization once someone asked me how I'm going to deal with bots. The idea was not a priority at all before.

replies.author: Niedzwiedz87
replies.body:
Then there's nothing to worry about.  
Maybe it'll slow down adoption, but in any case let's keep in mind Reddit tends to be an echo-chamber - in that case for AI hatred.

And I get AI hatred, I understand the haters, though their hatred might sometimes be misdirected.

But soon, practically all games will be developed with AI support so you can keep working on it, it's a great hobby I think.

comments.author: YYS770
comments.body:
"See all the hate". 

Reddit is an extremely biased community where MANY if not most of a single type of opinion will show up in condensed form. 

If I were to assume that typical Reddit opinion makes up any significant part of what the world as a whole thinks, I would have a very mistaken picture of those around me as I travel. 

Other than that, a vocal minority as the power to make themselves seem like much more than they really are. 

So I say this -   
Take what's bothering most people about AI from a pragmatic standpoint: slop, fake, cheap, unenjoyable, etc. and use that to understand what to avoid. It's similar to those 2d "artists" (wayy before AI) who made heavily digital-looking imitations of a single style on repeat. One look at it tells you that it's boring, uninteresting, shallow, and certainly not for your product. 

You can use AI VERY effectively while still putting in the same effort as always has been, and let the wolves howl at you from the park, while you ride away to success. 

Because a good game is appreciated and bought for having sold an actually enjoyable experience. Just make sure to take criticism seriously, especially when it comes to UX design (meaning, NOT just the UI parts, but the playability of your game's experience; that the tutorial/onboarding works FOR your game and not against it, that level design SUBTLY aids the player in figuring things out "on their own", and so forth).

comments.author: retrorays
comments.body: Op - you're concern shouldn't be that people do not wnat to play AI games. The issue is that anyone, and everyone, will be able to make AI games.

comments.author: Apalala__
comments.body:
[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZXsQAXx\_ao0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZXsQAXx_ao0)

And if you get criticism, use AI to read through the comments for you and filter out the noise. Let it identify the feedback that's actually useful so you can focus on improving your game instead of getting dragged into arguments.

comments.author: YKLKTMA
comments.body:
I’ll give you some advice on something else. Writing a detailed design document for a game that hasn’t even gone through prototyping yet is basically a waste of time. Most of what you wrote will end up in the trash, because things that sound good on paper often just don’t work in practice. That’s the first classic beginner mistake.

The second one is jumping straight into an online game when you don’t even have experience making something as simple as Pac-Man. It’s like not knowing how to ride a bicycle and immediately trying to fly a jumbo jet.

Start with simple games and go through the full development cycle from idea to commercial release several times before taking on anything more complex. And you can safely forget about making a large online game solo with no budget.

replies.author: panjezor
replies.body:
I do agree with the principle. I feel confident having built other services that I can at least make an attempt at tackling that. Writing the design docs may have been a mistake from a business perspective, however it brought me great joy just to think it through, so it's not like I wasted my time. At worst, it was some creative writing.

And to try that as someone who hasn't published a GAME before? I just enjoy diving in deep waters I guess.

I do appreciate the advice!

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: All beginners are confident. That’s basically the Dunning-Kruger effect. Their confidence is based on not knowing enough.

comments.author: PositiveScarcity8909
comments.body:
You are making a game you wanted to play 10 years ago, talking about 60 pages of gameplay features, socializing and monetization...

I think you got bigger things to worry about than AI hate.
